defaults.permitted_development: Across Dorset, roof-lights are often permitted development where they stay low-profile, project no more than 150mm from the roof plane and do not rise above the existing roof height. The straightforward route can disappear if the property is listed, subject to local restrictions or if the proposal starts to read as a roof enlargement rather than a simple skylight.

rules.height_rules: Across Dorset, a roof-light must not push the roof above the existing highest part. Keeping the frame low-profile and subordinate to the roof slope is usually the safest approach.
rules.depth_rules: Across Dorset, keep the projection tight to the existing slope. The normal roof-light limit is 150mm, and anything noticeably prouder than that risks being treated as a more substantial roof alteration.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Dorset, roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.
rules.roof_rules: Across Dorset, think of a roof-light as a small insertion into the existing slope, not as a way to reshape the roof. Larger additions, terraces and platforms are outside the ordinary roof-light allowance.
rules.materials_rules: Across Dorset, materials are not just about weathering: they control how visible the roof-light looks. Neat flashings, restrained frame colours and a low-profile unit usually sit better than bright trims or bulky cassettes.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof-lights on prominent roof slopes in conservation areas often face a closer design review, especially where they would affect a traditional roofscape or visible frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Installing roof-lights in a listed building, or altering historic roof fabric within its curtilage, can require listed building consent even where the unit looks modest.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions or roof-specific planning conditions can remove the usual householder right to add roof-lights, especially on visible elevations or in heritage areas.

rules.permitted_development: In Bournemouth Christchurch and Poole, a modest roof-light on a house is usually permitted development if it projects no more than 150mm from the existing roof slope, does not exceed the height of the existing roof and the property still benefits from normal householder rights. Planning permission becomes more likely where the work is on a listed building, in a controlled area or tied to a wider roof enlargement.

rules.height_rules: The alteration must not exceed the height of the existing roof. In practice that means choosing a low-profile unit that sits quietly within the roof slope rather than reading as an added structure on top of it.
rules.depth_rules: Keep the projection tight to the existing slope. The normal roof-light limit is 150mm, and anything noticeably prouder than that risks being treated as a more substantial roof alteration.
rules.boundary_rules: If the proposal creates a side-facing window, it should be obscure-glazed and any opening part should have its lowest edge at least 1.7 metres above the floor level of the room. Privacy and visible road-facing roof slopes deserve the earliest check.
rules.roof_rules: The proposal should read as a modest alteration to the existing roof rather than a new roof form in its own right. Roof terraces and larger enlargements are separate development types with stricter rules.
rules.materials_rules: Choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof-lights on prominent roof slopes in conservation areas often face a closer design review, especially where they would affect a traditional roofscape or visible frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: A listed building roof usually needs a heritage-led approach: even a small roof-light can require consent if it affects the historic fabric or appearance.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions or roof-specific planning conditions can remove the usual householder right to add roof-lights, especially on visible elevations or in heritage areas.
